excerpt: How to move a file with the mouse without copying it by accident, what happens between drives, and how to undo a drag that went to the wrong place.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to move files with the mouse without losing them. You will learn when a drag copies and when it moves, how to be sure before you let go, and how to undo a drag that landed in the wrong folder.
Dragging a file takes it from one place and puts it in another. Whether it moves or copies depends on where it came from: within one drive it moves, and between two drives it copies.
If the mouse still feels unnatural, take your time. Nothing you drag can be lost for good, and the file can always be put back.
You will see the file icon follow the pointer, and the folder under it highlight when it is ready to receive.
Before you start

items: Two folders open on screen, or one folder and the desktop.
One practice file you do not mind moving.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Drag, and watch before you let go
Nothing is lost by a drag that goes wrong, so there is no reason to fear the mouse. Press Escape or Ctrl and Z, and the file is exactly where it was.
The mouse tells you what it is about to do. Look at the small symbol beside the pointer before you release the button.

items: Click the file and hold the button down.
Move the pointer over the destination folder.
Read the small label beside the pointer: Copy to, or Move to.
Release the button to complete the action.
Press Escape before you release to cancel the drag.
Hold Ctrl while dragging to force a copy, or Shift to force a move.

body.text: You will see the folder highlight as you hover over it, and the file disappear from the first window once the drop completes. If the file is still in both places, the drag copied it, which is what happens between drives.

body.alt: A file being dragged between two folder windows.
body.caption: Hold, hover, read the label, then release. Escape cancels a drag that is going wrong.

body.text: It looks like dragging is the same everywhere. Between two drives it copies, and between two folders on one drive it moves, which is why a file sometimes stays where it was.
Move or copy on purpose
When you need certainty, use the keyboard instead of relying on the default.

items: Ctrl and C, then Ctrl and V: copies and leaves the original.
Ctrl and X, then Ctrl and V: moves and removes the original.
Both methods work across any two folders and any two drives.
Use copy for anything you are unsure about, and delete the leftover later.
For a whole folder, the same shortcuts work.
Check the destination before you close the window.

body.text: None of this is slower than dragging once you know the keys, and it removes the guesswork entirely.

body.alt: A hand dragging a file icon across a screen.
body.caption: The keyboard is the reliable version: copy, click the destination, paste, and check.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Most people drop a file in the wrong folder in their first week, and none of these fixes take more than a minute.

items: You dropped it in the wrong folder: press Ctrl and Z at once.
The file disappeared: it moved rather than copied. Search for its name, or check the folder you dragged it into.
You dropped it onto a program icon and it opened a copy: close the program, and check the file is still in its folder.
The drag will not start: you clicked outside the file, or the file is open in another program.
The pointer shows a crossed circle: the destination does not accept files, such as a program menu.
You moved a folder into itself: Windows refuses this, and the folder stays where it was.

body.text: Practice
Three drags and two keyboard moves, and the difference is clear.

items: Make two folders on the desktop, and put a test file in one.
Drag the file to the other folder and watch which label appears.
Press Ctrl and drag, and see the label change to copy.
Move a file with Ctrl and X, then Ctrl and V.
Undo one move with Ctrl and Z.

body.text: You can now move files without fear of losing them, because you know how to cancel and how to undo. In the next lesson you will write a CV that fits on one page and tells the truth.

excerpt: How to write a one-page CV with no experience gap, what to include when you are starting out, and the three things that make an employer call.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to write a one-page CV that a busy employer can read in thirty seconds. You will structure it, fill it with honest evidence, and save it as a PDF that opens anywhere. You do not need experience to have a CV worth reading.
A CV is not a life story. It is an argument that you can do the job, made in one page, with evidence a reader can check. Everything that does not support that argument is in the way of it.
If you have never written one, that is normal. Most people write their first CV in an afternoon, and nobody expects it to be finished in one draft.
Before you start

items: A document program, such as Word or Google Docs.
One uninterrupted hour, and paper to plan on.
The dates of your schooling, any training, and any work, including informal work.

body.text: The seven parts, in order
Nigerian employers expect this order, and following it means nothing gets lost.

items: Your name, in large type, then your phone number and email address on one line.
A profile of two lines saying what you do and what you are looking for.
Education, newest first, with dates and the qualification.
Experience, newest first, including informal work, family business, and volunteering.
Skills that are true and useful, such as typing speed, Excel, or spoken languages.
One or two references, with a phone number and their permission.
Nothing else. No photograph unless the employer asks, no date of birth, no marital status.

body.text: You will see the page fill faster than you expect. If it spills onto a second page, cut the oldest schooling detail rather than shrinking the font.

body.alt: A one page CV with a clear name and short sections.
body.caption: Name, profile, education, experience, skills. One page, one font, and white space between sections.

body.text: It looks like a longer CV shows more effort. A two-page CV from a beginner usually shows padding, and a reader notices the gaps rather than the effort.
Fill it when you have little experience
Most first CVs are thin on formal work. That is normal, and it does not leave the page empty.

items: Name the work you did even if it was unpaid: helping in a family shop, teaching a younger cousin, running errands for a business.
Describe what you did with a number where you can: served about thirty customers a day.
List training and certificates, including short courses and any academy sessions completed.
Name your skills honestly: typing at 35 words a minute is stronger than fast typing.
Include school leadership, a team, or a society only if it shows something the job needs.
Leave out hobbies that say nothing about work, and leave out anything you cannot discuss if asked.

body.text: None of this is invention. The same small jobs described concretely read as experience, while a list of adjectives reads as a template.

body.alt: A printed CV on a table beside a pen.
body.caption: Print one copy and read it in your hand. Typos you missed on screen appear immediately on paper.

body.text: The three things that get a call
Employers skim. Three details decide whether they read the rest.

items: A phone number that is correct and answered politely.
Evidence that matches the job advertisement, using the words it uses.
No spelling mistakes, especially in your own name and the employer's.
A tidy layout: one font, aligned dates, and consistent spacing.
A file name that says who you are: ada-okoro-cv.pdf.
Sent as a PDF, so the layout cannot move on their computer.

body.text: Do not worry about not having the perfect background. An honest, clear, one-page CV from a beginner beats a padded one from anybody, and employers in small firms read every one.
If it goes wrong
Each of these is fixable before you send, and the last one is asked about most.

items: It will not fit on one page: cut the oldest detail, reduce the margins to 2 cm, and keep the font at 11 or 12.
The layout moves on another computer: you sent a .docx instead of a PDF.
You have no references: ask a teacher, a pastor, or a former customer, and ask their permission first.
You cannot remember exact dates: use the month and the year, which is accurate enough.
The file is too large to email: it probably contains photographs. Remove them, or export again.
You have a gap in your dates: state it honestly, such as caring for a family member, rather than filling it with a false entry.

body.text: Practice
Write it in one sitting, then leave it a day before you send it.

items: Write the seven sections on paper first, with dates.
Type it in Word with one font at 11 or 12 point.
Cut it to one page, and check the margins.
Save it as a PDF named with your own name.
Print one copy, read it aloud, and ask somebody else to read it too.

body.text: You can now hand an employer a page that respects their time and gives them a reason to call. In the next chapter the series moves to the shop counter, where a spreadsheet earns its keep.

excerpt: How to format a column as naira so it reads as money, why the currency belongs in the format and not the cell, and how to keep totals adding correctly.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to make a column of numbers read as money: ₦1,500.00 instead of 1500. You will set the format, choose how many decimals to show, and keep the total adding correctly. It takes five minutes, and it makes a sheet look like a record rather than a list.
Formatting changes how a number looks, not what it is. The cell still holds 1500, so formulas still add it. This is the whole reason to use formatting rather than typing the sign yourself.
Before you start

items: A spreadsheet with a column of amounts.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Format the column, not each cell

items: Type the amounts as plain numbers first: 1500, not N1,500.
Select the whole column, or only the cells you need.
Open Format, then Number, then Currency, in Excel or Google Sheets.
Choose the naira symbol if it is offered, or type it in the format field.
Set two decimal places for money, or none if you never record kobo.
Look at the formula bar: it still shows 1500, which proves the number is unchanged.

body.text: You will see the same figures now displayed with the sign, commas, and decimals, and they stay lined up on the right of the cell. That right alignment is how you know they are still numbers.
The Format Cells box will open with a list of categories down the left side, and Currency near the top of that list. A preview line at the bottom shows exactly how your number will look.

body.alt: A spreadsheet column formatted as currency with a naira symbol.
body.caption: Format the column once. Every new number typed into it takes the same money format.

body.text: It looks like typing the naira sign shows the sheet is professional. Typing it turns the number into text, the total ignores it, and the change takes a hundred keystrokes instead of one.
Several currencies in one sheet
If you invoice in naira and sometimes receive dollars, the format can hold the distinction without mixing the sums.

items: Keep one currency per column, and name the column for it, such as Amount in naira.
Use a separate column for the exchange rate, so the arithmetic is visible.
Format the dollar column with a dollar sign, using the same method.
Never add a naira total to a dollar total, even if the numbers look similar.
Record the rate you used and the date, because the rate changes.
Round only at the end, not at every step, or the totals drift.

body.text: None of this needs a second sheet. Two columns and one rate cell are enough for a small business, and they keep the record honest.

body.alt: A spreadsheet showing a naira amount column and a total.
body.caption: One currency per column, formatted as money. The total then reads as money too.

body.text: Decimals, rounding, and kobo
Money needs a consistent number of decimals, and small choices here cause the disagreements.

items: Choose two decimals if you record kobo, and none if you round to the naira.
Keep the same choice in every column of the same sheet.
A total of 1,500.0000001 means the arithmetic used fractions. Round the display to two.
Add the sum with =SUM(range) rather than typing it, so the display and the maths agree.
For a price list, show no decimals, which reads faster at a counter.
For an invoice, show two, because a customer will check.

body.text: Do not worry about the formatting looking different when somebody else opens the file. The format travels with the spreadsheet, and a PDF keeps it exactly.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a formatting fix, and your figures are never changed by it.

items: The total does not include some numbers: those cells are text. Retype one and watch the total move.
The column shows a strange date: the numbers were read as dates. Reformat the cells as Currency.
Everything shows many decimals: the format is set to General. Choose Currency with two decimals.
The sign is missing on new rows: the format applies to selected cells only. Copy the format down.
The numbers are left aligned: they are stored as text. Clear the cell and retype without a sign or space.
Printing shows #### instead of the total: the column is too narrow. Widen it.

body.text: Practice
One column, formatted once, and the sheet looks like a record.

items: Type five amounts as plain numbers.
Select the column and apply a currency format with two decimals.
Click one cell and confirm the formula bar shows the plain number.
Add a total with =SUM and check it displays as money.
Print or preview the sheet and confirm the sign appears.

body.text: You can now present figures that read as money and still calculate correctly. In the next lesson you will keep the heading visible while you scroll through a long list.

excerpt: How to keep the header row visible while you scroll, freeze a name column as well, and turn it off again when somebody needs the whole sheet.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to freeze the top row of a spreadsheet so the headings stay visible as you scroll. You will freeze a row, freeze two columns, and unfreeze when you are done. On a list of two hundred rows, it is the difference between working and guessing.
Freezing pins rows or columns in place while the rest scrolls underneath. It changes nothing in the data, and it is stored with the file, so the next person who opens it sees the same view.
Before you start

items: A spreadsheet with a header row and at least thirty rows of data.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Freeze the header

items: Click a cell directly below the header row, in the first data row.
Open View, then Freeze panes, then Freeze rows above, in Excel or Sheets.
Scroll down and confirm the header stays at the top.
To freeze the first column as well, click a cell below and to the right of both.
Choose Freeze panes rather than Freeze top row when you need both.
To undo it, choose Unfreeze from the same menu.

body.text: You will see a thin grey line under the frozen row and the header remain in place while the rest scrolls under it. That line is the only visible mark, and it does not print.
The View menu will open with Freeze panes in the middle of the list, and a small arrow beside it for the choices. Moving the pointer over each choice shows a short description of what it locks.

body.alt: A spreadsheet with the top row frozen and a grey line beneath it.
body.caption: A thin grey line marks where the freeze begins. The header stays, and everything below scrolls.

body.text: It looks like freezing is a permanent change to the file. It is a view, like a zoom, and it can be switched off in two clicks.
Freeze a name column too
A wide list of customers has names on the left and figures far to the right. Freezing both keeps the row and the person identifiable.

items: Put the important identifier, such as the name, in the first column.
Click the cell directly below and to the right of the header block.
Choose Freeze panes, which pins everything above and to the left of that cell.
Scroll right and confirm the name column stays visible.
Scroll down and confirm the header stays visible.
Unfreeze before you send the file to somebody who needs a clean view.

body.text: None of this affects formulas, sorting, or printing. It only changes what stays on screen while you move around the sheet.

body.alt: A spreadsheet scrolled down with the header row still visible.
body.caption: Header frozen, list scrolled to row ninety. The reader still knows which column is which.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a view fix, and none of them touches your figures.

items: The freeze is in the wrong place: unfreeze, then click a cell in the right position and freeze again.
You cannot find the option: it is under View, not Format or Data.
The lines disappeared: another freeze or a filter was applied. Reset the view.
The frozen row scrolls away: the freeze was applied to a selection, not a pane. Unfreeze and repeat.
Printing now shows a repeated header: that is a separate print-title setting, and it is helpful.
A colleague finds the sheet odd: unfreeze before you share it, and let them choose.

body.text: Practice
Freeze, scroll, unfreeze, and the habit is clear.

items: Open a long list and scroll to the bottom before freezing.
Freeze the header row and repeat the scroll.
Freeze the name column as well and scroll sideways.
Unfreeze everything and check the sheet looks normal.
Save and reopen the file to confirm the freeze was kept.

body.text: You can now read a long list without losing your place. In the next lesson you will use one formula for a whole column instead of typing it forty times.

excerpt: A five-minute weekly record of money in and money out, what columns it needs, and how to read it honestly at the end of the week.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to build a simple weekly money list: what came in, what went out, and what is left. You will set it up in ten minutes and keep it in three minutes a day. You do not need accounting experience, only honesty and a habit.

A money list is not a budget you fail at. It is a record of what actually happened, written down the day it happened. Once the week is visible, the decisions become obvious without anybody telling you what to do.
Before you start

items: A spreadsheet, on a computer or a phone.
Ten minutes, and your memory of the last two days.
A pen and paper if you prefer to plan before typing.

body.text: The columns that matter

items: Date: the day the money moved.
What: a short description, such as transport or sales.
In: money received, entered as a plain number.
Out: money spent.
Category: one or two words, such as food, transport, stock, family.
Balance: a formula that keeps a running total.

body.text: You will see the table look too simple to be useful at first. After seven days it becomes a picture of the week, and the categories tell you more than the total.

body.alt: A spreadsheet showing a weekly money list with in and out columns.
body.caption: Date, what, in, out, category. Five columns answer the question where the week went.

body.text: The sheet will open with your six columns across the top and an empty row waiting underneath, and the cursor will sit in the first cell ready for today's date.
It looks like a money list needs an app with bank connections. A plain sheet you fill in yourself is more reliable in a week with cash sales and one shared phone.
Set up the totals

items: Under the In and Out columns, add =SUM for each.
Add a row called Left with a formula subtracting Out from In.
Add a category total using =SUMIF, which adds only the rows matching a category.
Format the money columns as naira, with no decimals for cash.
Freeze the header row so it stays visible as the week grows.
Add a new row at the top of the list each day, so the newest is first.

body.text: None of this needs a second sheet. One table, three formulas, and the week adds itself.

body.alt: A simple money list on paper beside a phone showing the same list.
body.caption: Paper and sheet both work. What matters is writing it on the day, not after three weeks.

body.text: Read it honestly
The value comes from reading it without excuses. A money list you argue with is still more useful than one you do not have.

items: At the end of the week, look at the category totals rather than the grand total.
Find the one category that grew without a reason, and name it.
Compare two weeks before you conclude anything.
Record cash as carefully as transfers, because cash is where the gaps hide.
Keep one row for a bill that arrives monthly, so it does not surprise you.
Do not adjust last week's numbers to look better. The record is the point.

body.text: Do not worry about a bad week. A record that shows a bad week is doing its job, and it is the reason the next one is better.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a correction, and the first one causes most of them.

items: The total is lower than expected: some numbers are stored as text. Retype one and watch the total move.
The balance goes negative for no reason: a spend was typed into the In column.
Categories are spelled three ways: choose from one list, and fix the spellings once.
You missed three days: enter them from memory, marked with an approximate note, rather than leaving gaps.
The sheet is on one phone and you use another: use a cloud sheet, or keep a paper copy.
You stopped after two weeks: reduce it to one line a day, which is enough to keep the habit.

body.text: Practice
Build it today, fill in two days, and decide tomorrow whether it stays.

items: Build the six columns and the three totals.
Enter today's money in and out, honestly.
Add yesterday from memory, marked as approximate.
Format the money columns and freeze the header.
Look at the category totals and name the one you would change.

body.text: You can now see a week of money instead of remembering it. In the next lesson you will read the error messages a spreadsheet shows and fix them without panic.
